hook_text: The chicken on your plate was probably six weeks old, and the maize in your pap may make its own insecticide.
clip_script: Inside a shed as long as a football field, tens of thousands of chickens grow to full size in about six weeks. That's factory farming. It's why chicken and eggs are some of the cheapest protein in South Africa. But crowded animals suffer. Bird flu spreads fast. Antibiotics overused on farms can create superbugs. Now look at a maize field. Scientists added a gene from a soil bacterium, so the plant fights off caterpillars by itself. Most of South Africa's maize is grown this way. Fewer sprays, bigger harvests. But insects can evolve resistance, and a few big companies own the seeds. So are these technologies heroes or villains? Neither. Put the evidence on the scale, and decide for yourself.
visual_style: Rows of chickens in a vast lit shed; eggs rolling on a conveyor; cattle in a feedlot; a microscope view of bacteria; a scientist in a lab inserting a gene; a maize field with a caterpillar on a leaf; a balance scale weighing benefits and risks.
pacing: Brisk facts, then a balanced pause at the end.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to weigh up factory farming and genetically modified crops.
